Raise KeyError for missing paths, ValueError for unknown filters.", "action": {"tool": "write_file", "args": {"path": "src/textkit/render_template.py", "content": "from __future__ import annotations

import re
from typing import Any, Mapping


_FILTERS = {
    "upper": str.upper,
    "lower": str.lower,
    "title": str.title,
    "trim": str.strip,
}

_PLACEHOLDER_RE = re.compile(r"\{\{(.+?)\}\}")


def render_template(template: str, context: Mapping[str, Any]) -> str:
    """
    Render "{{ ... }}" placeholders in a notification/email template.

    Placeholder syntax: "{{" name ("|" filter)* "}}", with optional whitespace
    around the name, the filters and the bars. `name` is a dotted path looked up in
    `context` through nested mappings: "user.first_name" means
    context["user"]["first_name"]. The value is converted with str() and the
    filters are applied left to right. Supported filters: upper, lower, title
    (str.title) and trim (str.strip). Text outside placeholders is copied
    unchanged.

    Errors:
      * KeyError if any part of the path is missing, or if a non-mapping value
        would have to be indexed.
      * ValueError for an unknown filter name.

    Examples:
        render_template("Hi {{ user.name | title }}!", {"user": {"name": "ada"}}) == "Hi Ada!"
        render_template("{{count}} new", {"count": 3}) == "3 new"
    """
    def _resolve(path: str, ctx: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Any:
        parts = path.strip().split(".")
        current: Any = ctx
        for part in parts:
            if not isinstance(current, Mapping):
                raise KeyError(
                    f"Cannot index into non-mapping value at path '{part}'"
                )
            if part not in current:
                raise KeyError(f"Key '{part}' not found in context")
            current = current[part]
        return current

    def _render_inner(inner: str) -> str:
        # Split on | to separate name and filters
        segments = [seg.strip() for seg in inner.split("|")]
        name = segments[0]
        filters = segments[1:]

        value = _resolve(name, context)
        result = str(value)

        for f in filters:
            if f not in _FILTERS:
                raise ValueError(f"Unknown filter: '{f}'")
            result = _FILTERS[f](result)

        return result

    def _replace(match: re.Match) -> str:
        return _render_inner(match.group(1))

    return _PLACEHOLDER_RE.sub(_replace, template)
"}}, "messages": []}

from typing import Any, Sequence


def join_human(items: Sequence[Any], conjunction: str = "and") -> str:
    """
    Join `items` into a human-readable English list for UI copy such as
    "Liked by Ana, Ben and 3 others".

      * no items -> ""
      * one item -> that item
      * two items -> "A and B"
      * three or more -> the items separated by ", ", with the conjunction placed
        before the last item

    Items are converted with str() and used as-is (no trimming). `conjunction`
    replaces "and", e.g. conjunction="or".

    Examples:
        join_human(["tea"]) == "tea"
        join_human(["tea", "coffee"], conjunction="or") == "tea or coffee"
    """
    strs = [str(item) for item in items]
    if len(strs) == 0:
        return ""
    if len(strs) == 1:
        return strs[0]
    if len(strs) == 2:
        return f"{strs[0]} {conjunction} {strs[1]}"
    return ", ".join(strs[:-1]) + f" {conjunction} {strs[-1]}"
"}}, "messages": []}

def edit_distance(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    """
    Return the edit distance between `a` and `b`: the minimum number of
    single-character edits needed to turn `a` into `b`.

    Inserting, deleting or substituting one character each cost 1. The comparison
    is case-sensitive, and the distance is symmetric:
    edit_distance(a, b) == edit_distance(b, a). Used by search suggestions for
    typo tolerance.

    Examples:
        edit_distance("kitten", "sitting") == 3
        edit_distance("", "abc") == 3
    """
    if len(a) < len(b):
        a, b = b, a

    prev = list(range(len(b) + 1))
    for i, ca in enumerate(a):
        curr = [i + 1]
        for j, cb in enumerate(b):
            cost = 0 if ca == cb else 1
            curr.append(min(prev[j + 1] + 1, curr[j] + 1, prev[j] + cost))
        prev = curr
    return prev[len(b)]
"}}, "messages": []}

I'll write the full file.", "action": {"tool": "write_file", "args": {"path": "src/textkit/normalize_whitespace.py", "content": "from __future__ import annotations

import re

# Zero-width / invisible characters that must be removed outright (no space
# is inserted where they appear). These come in with text pasted from
# rich-text editors.
_INVISIBLE = "\u200b\u200c\u200d\u2060\ufeff"
_INVISIBLE_RE = re.compile("[" + _INVISIBLE + "]")
_WHITESPACE_RE = re.compile(r"\s+")


def normalize_whitespace(text: str) -> str:
    """
    Collapse every run of whitespace in `text` into a single ASCII space and
    strip leading and trailing whitespace.

    "Whitespace" means any character for which str.isspace() is true: spaces, tabs,
    newlines, non-breaking spaces (U+00A0), em spaces and so on. This is the first
    cleanup step applied to titles, excerpts and user-submitted copy.

    Invisible zero-width characters that come in with text pasted from rich-text
    editors are deleted outright: U+200B (zero width space), U+200C, U+200D,
    U+2060 (word joiner) and U+FEFF (byte order mark). They are not treated as
    whitespace, so no space is inserted where they were.

    Examples:
        normalize_whitespace("  Hello \\t\\n world  ") == "Hello world"
        normalize_whitespace("") == ""
        normalize_whitespace("co\u200bop") == "coop"
        normalize_whitespace("\ufeffTitle") == "Title"
    """
    text = _INVISIBLE_RE.sub("", text)
    return _WHITESPACE_RE.sub(" ", text).strip()"}}, "messages": []}

import unicodedata
from typing import List, Optional

from .tokenize_words import tokenize_words


def slugify(text: str, max_length: Optional[int] = None) -> str:
    """
    Build a URL slug from a title.

    The text is split into words with tokenize_words(). Each word is reduced to
    ASCII by stripping diacritics (Unicode NFKD decomposition, then dropping
    non-ASCII characters), after which any remaining character other than a-z and
    0-9 is removed; words that end up empty are discarded. The remaining words are
    joined with "-", so the slug only contains a-z, 0-9 and "-".

    If `max_length` is given, the slug is shortened to at most max_length
    characters and never ends with "-". Raises ValueError if max_length is given
    and is < 1.

    Examples:
        slugify("Hello, World!") == "hello-world"
        slugify("Crème Brûlée Recipes") == "creme-brulee-recipes"
        slugify("50% off: Summer Sale") == "50-off-summer-sale"
    """
    if max_length is not None and max_length < 1:
        raise ValueError("max_length must be >= 1")

    words: List[str] = []
    for word in tokenize_words(text):
        decomposed = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", word)
        ascii_word = "".join(ch for ch in decomposed if ord(ch) < 128)
        cleaned = "".join(ch for ch in ascii_word if ch.isalnum())
        if cleaned:
            words.append(cleaned)

    if not words:
        return ""

    if max_length is None:
        return "-".join(words)

    # Keep as many whole words as fit within max_length (words joined by "-
    # consume one extra char each). Only cut the first word if it alone exceeds
    # max_length.
    if len(words[0]) <= max_length:
        kept: List[str] = [words[0]]
        used = len(words[0])
        for w in words[1:]:
            if used + 1 + len(w) <= max_length:
                kept.append(w)
                used += 1 + len(w)
        return "-".join(kept)

    return words[0][:max_length]
"}}, "messages": []}

import re

# Zero-width / invisible characters that must be removed outright (no space
# is inserted where they appear). These come in with text pasted from
# rich-text editors.
_INVISIBLE = "\u200b\u200c\u200d\u2060\ufeff"
_INVISIBLE_RE = re.compile("[" + _INVISIBLE + "]")
_WHITESPACE_RE = re.compile(r"\s+")


def normalize_whitespace(text: str) -> str:
    """
    Collapse every run of whitespace in `text` into a single ASCII space and
    strip leading and trailing whitespace.

    "Whitespace" means any character for which str.isspace() is true: spaces, tabs,
    newlines, non-breaking spaces (U+00A0), em spaces and so on. This is the first
    cleanup step applied to titles, excerpts and user-submitted copy.

    Invisible zero-width characters that come in with text pasted from rich-text
    editors are deleted outright: U+200B (zero width space), U+200C, U+200D,
    U+2060 (word joiner) and U+FEFF (byte order mark). They are not treated as
    whitespace, so no space is inserted where they were.

    Examples:
        normalize_whitespace("  Hello \\t\\n world  ") == "Hello world"
        normalize_whitespace("") == ""
        normalize_whitespace("co\u200bop") == "coop"
        normalize_whitespace("\ufeffTitle") == "Title"
    """
    text = _INVISIBLE_RE.sub("", text)
    return _WHITESPACE_RE.sub(" ", text).strip()"}}, "messages": []}

from typing import List

from .tokenize_words import tokenize_words

_MINOR_WORDS = frozenset({"a", "an", "for", "in", "of", "on", "the", "to"})


def make_acronym(phrase: str) -> str:
    """
    Build an acronym from the first character of each word of `phrase`.

    Words come from tokenize_words(), so hyphenated parts count as separate words
    ("self-contained" contributes "SC"). Letters are upper-cased; a word that starts
    with a digit contributes that digit. Returns "" when the phrase has no words.

    Minor words (a, an, for, in, of, on, the, to) that are not the first word keep
    their letter in lower case.

    Examples:
        make_acronym("Portable Network Graphics") == "PNG"
        make_acronym("self-contained underwater breathing apparatus") == "SCUBA"
        make_acronym("Department of Defense") == "DoD"
        make_acronym("The Lord of the Rings") == "TLotR"
    """
    words: List[str] = tokenize_words(phrase)
    if not words:
        return ""

    parts: List[str] = []
    for i, word in enumerate(words):
        ch = word[0]
        if i > 0 and word in _MINOR_WORDS:
            parts.append(ch)  # keep lowercase
        else:
            parts.append(ch.upper())
    return "".join(parts)

from typing import Any, Dict, Iterable, List, Mapping, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple, Union

from .split_identifier import split_identifier


def to_camel_case(name: str, upper_first: bool = False) -> str:
    """
    Convert an identifier written in any naming convention to camelCase, or to
    PascalCase when `upper_first` is True.

    The words come from split_identifier(). The first word stays lowercase
    (capitalized when upper_first=True); every following word is capitalized
    (first character upper case, the rest lower case). Words are concatenated
    without separators. Returns "" when there are no words.

    The output is used as a generated JSON/JavaScript field name, so it must
    be a valid identifier: if the result would start with a digit, a single
    underscore is prefixed.

    Examples:
        to_camel_case("user_account_id") == "userAccountId"
        to_camel_case("user_account_id", upper_first=True) == "UserAccountId"
        to_camel_case("3d_model") == "_3dModel"
        to_camel_case("2fa-enabled", upper_first=True) == "_2faEnabled"
    """
    words = split_identifier(name)
    if not words:
        return ""

    if upper_first:
        result = words[0].capitalize() + "".join(w.capitalize() for w in words[1:])
    else:
        result = words[0] + "".join(w.capitalize() for w in words[1:])

    if result and result[0].isdigit():
        result = "_" + result

    return result

from typing import List

from .normalize_whitespace import normalize_whitespace

_TERMINATORS = set(".!")
_TERMINATORS_WITH_Q = set(".!? ")
_ABBREVIATIONS = {"Mr.", "Mrs.", "Ms.", "Dr.", "Prof.", "St.", "vs.", "e.g.", "i.e."}
_CLOSING = set('"\')])')
_OPENING = set('"\'([')


def _strip_closing(word: str) -> str:
    """Remove trailing closing quotes/brackets from a word."""
    i = len(word)
    while i > 0 and word[i - 1] in _CLOSING:
        i -= 1
    return word[:i]


def _ends_with_terminator(core: str) -> bool:
    """True if core ends with a run of . ! ? chars."""
    if not core:
        return False
    return core[-1] in ".!?"


def _is_initial(core: str) -> bool:
    """True if core is a single uppercase letter + '.', optionally after an opening quote/bracket."""
    s = core
    if s and s[0] in _OPENING:
        s = s[1:]
    return len(s) == 2 and s[0].isupper() and s[1] == "."


def _is_abbreviation(core: str) -> bool:
    return core in _ABBREVIATIONS


def _starts_boundary(word: str) -> bool:
    if not word:
        return False
    first = word[0]
    return first.isupper() or first.isdigit() or first in _OPENING

    """
    Split prose into sentences.

    The text is first cleaned with normalize_whitespace() and then split into
    space-separated words. A word ends a sentence when:

import re


def tokenize_words(text: str) -> List[str]:
    """
    Split `text` into lowercase word tokens, in order of appearance.

    words such as "café" or "naïve" are single tokens. Whitespace and
    punctuation (including underscores and hyphens) separate tokens and are

from typing import List


def split_csv_line(line: str, delimiter: str = ",") -> List[str]:
    """
    Split one line of CSV into its fields (used by the bulk tag importer).

      * Fields are separated by `delimiter`, a single character other than '"'.
      * A field may be enclosed in double quotes; inside a quoted field the
        delimiter is literal and a doubled quote ("") stands for one '"'.
      * Unquoted fields are returned exactly as written (no trimming).
      * Spaces between a delimiter (or the start of the line) and an opening
        quote are skipped and the field is parsed as quoted.
      * An empty line gives [""]; a trailing delimiter gives a trailing empty field.

    Raises ValueError for an unterminated quoted field, for any text between a
    closing quote and the next delimiter, and for an invalid delimiter (not exactly
    one character, or '"').

    Examples:
        split_csv_line('a,"b,c",d') == ["a", "b,c", "d"]
        split_csv_line('x,"say ""hi"" now"') == ["x", 'say "hi" now']
    """
    if len(delimiter) != 1 or delimiter == '"':
        raise ValueError("delimiter must be a single character other than '\"'")

    if line == "":
        return [""]

    fields: List[str] = []
    i = 0
    n = len(line)
    first = True

    while True:
        # Skip leading spaces before an opening quote (only when we are at the
        # start of a field, i.e. after a delimiter or at the start of the line).
        while i < n and line[i] == " ":
            # Only skip if the next non-space char is a quote.
            j = i
            while j < n and line[j] == " ":
                j += 1
            if j < n and line[j] == '"':
                i = j
                break
            else:
                break

        if i < n and line[i] == '"':
            # Quoted field
            i += 1  # consume opening quote
            buf: List[str] = []
            closed = False
            while i < n:
                c = line[i]
                if c == '"':
                    if i + 1 < n and line[i + 1] == '"':
                        buf.append('"')
                        i += 2
                    else:
                        # closing quote
                        i += 1
                        closed = True
                        break
                else:
                    buf.append(c)
                    i += 1
            if not closed:
                raise ValueError("unterminated quoted field")
            # After closing quote, next char must be delimiter or end of line.
            if i < n and line[i] != delimiter:
                raise ValueError("unexpected text after closing quote")
            fields.append("".join(buf))
        else:
            # Unquoted field: read until delimiter or end.
            start = i
            while i < n and line[i] != delimiter:
                i += 1
            fields.append(line[start:i])

        if i >= n:
            break
        # line[i] == delimiter
        i += 1

    return fields

from typing import Any, Dict, Iterable, List, Mapping, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple, Union


def extract_headings(markdown: str) -> List[Tuple[int, str]]:
    """
    List the ATX headings of a Markdown document as (level, title) pairs, in
    document order.

    A heading line has at most 3 leading spaces, then 1-6 "#" characters, then
    either the end of the line or at least one space/tab followed by the title.
    The title has surrounding whitespace removed, and an optional closing run of
    "#" characters is dropped when it is preceded by a space or is the whole title.
    "#hashtag" (no space) and "####### seven" are not headings; a bare "#" is a
    level-1 heading with an empty title. Lines are split with str.splitlines().

    Example:
        extract_headings("# Intro\\ntext\\n## Setup ##\\n") == [(1, "Intro"), (2, "Setup")]
    """
    import re

    # Pattern: up to 3 leading spaces, 1-6 hashes, then either end-of-line or whitespace + title
    heading_re = re.compile(r'^ {0,3}(#{1,6})(?:[ \t]+(.*))?$')

    results: List[Tuple[int, str]] = []
    for line in markdown.splitlines():
        m = heading_re.match(line)
        if m is None:
            continue
        level = len(m.group(1))
        raw_title = m.group(2)
        if raw_title is None:
            title = ""
        else:
            title = raw_title.strip()
            # Drop optional closing run of '#' chars when preceded by space or is the whole title
            if title:
                # Check if title ends with a run of # chars preceded by a space
                stripped = re.sub(r'[ \t]+#+$', '', title)
                if stripped != title:
                    title = stripped.strip()
                # If the whole title is just # chars, drop them
                if title and re.fullmatch(r'#+', title):
                    title = ""
        results.append((level, title))
    return results

from .split_identifier import split_identifier


def to_snake_case(name: str) -> str:
    """Convert an identifier to snake_case.

    The identifier is split into its component words (see ``split_identifier``)
    and the words are joined with single underscores, lower-cased.

    Leading underscores mark private or internal names and are preserved
    exactly as they appear (e.g. ``"_cachedValue" -> "_cached_value"``,
    ``"__InitHook" -> "__init_hook"``). Trailing underscores are dropped
    (e.g. ``"trailing_" -> "trailing"``).
    """

    leading = len(name) - len(name.lstrip("_"))
    stripped = name[leading:]

    words = split_identifier(stripped)
    if not words:
        return "_" * leading

    return "_" * leading + "_".join(word.lower() for word in words)

from typing import List

from textkit.normalize_whitespace import normalize_whitespace


def wrap_text(text: str, width: int) -> List[str]:
    """
    Greedy word-wrap `text` into lines of at most `width` characters (used for
    plain-text emails).

    The text is cleaned with normalize_whitespace() and split into words on spaces.
    Words are added to the current line, separated by single spaces, as long as the
    line stays within `width`; otherwise a new line is started with that word. Lines
    have no leading or trailing spaces. Empty or whitespace-only text gives [].
    Raises ValueError if width < 1.

    Example:
        wrap_text("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", 10)
            == ["the quick", "brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy", "dog"]
    """
    if width < 1:
        raise ValueError("width must be >= 1")

    cleaned = normalize_whitespace(text)
    if not cleaned:
        return []

    words = cleaned.split(" ")
    lines: List[str] = []
    current = ""

    for word in words:
        if not current:
            current = word
        elif len(current) + 1 + len(word) <= width:
            current = current + " " + word
        else:
            lines.append(current)
            current = word

    if current:
        lines.append(current)

    return lines

Implement rank_matches: validate limit>=0, dedupe preserving order, compute score, filter >= min_score, sort by score desc with stable tie-break by original order, take limit.", "action": {"tool": "write_file", "args": {"path": "src/textkit/rank_matches.py", "content": "from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

from textkit.similarity import similarity


def rank_matches(query: str, candidates: Sequence[str], limit: int = 5, min_score: float = 0.0) -> List[Tuple[str, float]]:
    """
    Rank `candidates` by how closely they match `query` and return the best ones
    as (candidate, score) pairs, best score first. Used by the tag picker.

    The score of a candidate is similarity(query, candidate). Candidates scoring
    below `min_score` are dropped, then at most `limit` pairs are returned.
    Duplicate candidate strings are only ranked once. `candidates` is not modified.
    Raises ValueError if limit < 0.

    Example:
        rank_matches("python", ["java", "python", "pythons"], limit=2)
            == [("python", 1.0), ("pythons", 0.86)]
    """
    if limit < 0:
        raise ValueError("limit must be >= 0")

    # Deduplicate while preserving first-occurrence order.
    seen: set = set()
    unique: List[str] = []
    for cand in candidates:
        if cand not in seen:
            seen.add(cand)
            unique.append(cand)

    scored: List[Tuple[str, float]] = []
    for cand in unique:
        score = similarity(query, cand)
        if score >= min_score:
            scored.append((cand, score))

    # Sort by score descending; stable sort keeps original order for ties.
    scored.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)

    return scored[:limit]
"}}, "messages": []}

Now I'll implement top_words: tokenize, filter stopwords (case-insensitive) and digit-only tokens, count, sort by count desc then word asc, return top k.","action":{"tool":"write_file","args":{"path":"src/textkit/top_words.py","content":"from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from typing import Iterable, List, Optional, Tuple

from .tokenize_words import tokenize_words


def top_words(text: str, k: int, stopwords: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None) -> List[Tuple[str, int]]:
    """
    Return the `k` most frequent words of `text` as (word, count) pairs, most
    frequent first. Feeds the "top terms" panel of the article analytics page.

    Words come from tokenize_words(). Words listed in `stopwords` (compared
    case-insensitively) are ignored, and so are tokens made only of digits. If fewer
    than k distinct words remain, all of them are returned. Raises ValueError if
    k < 0.

    Examples:
        top_words("b a b c b a", 2) == [("b", 3), ("a", 2)]
        top_words("Data, data and more DATA", 1, stopwords=["and"]) == [("data", 3)]
    """
    if k < 0:
        raise ValueError("k must be >= 0")

    stop = {w.lower() for w in stopwords} if stopwords is not None else set()

    counts: Counter = Counter()
    for token in tokenize_words(text):
        if token in stop:
            continue
        if token.isdigit():
            continue
        counts[token] += 1

    ranked = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))

Let me rewrite the function with fence tracking.", "action": {"tool": "write_file", "args": {"path": "src/textkit/extract_headings.py", "content": "from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Tuple


def extract_headings(markdown: str) -> List[Tuple[int, str]]:
    """
    List the ATX headings of a Markdown document as (level, title) pairs, in
    document order.

    A heading line has at most 3 leading spaces, then 1-6 "#" characters, then
    either the end of the line or at least one space/tab followed by the title.
    The title has surrounding whitespace removed, and an optional closing run of
    "#" characters is dropped when it is preceded by a space or is the whole title.
    "#hashtag" (no space) and "####### seven" are not headings; a bare "#" is a
    level-1 heading with an empty title. Lines are split with str.splitlines().

    Fenced code blocks (opened and closed with ``` or ~~~, with at most 3
    leading spaces) are skipped entirely — lines inside a fence are never
    treated as headings.

    Example:
        extract_headings("# Intro\\ntext\\n## Setup ##\\n") == [(1, "Intro"), (2, "Setup")]
    """
    import re

    heading_re = re.compile(r'^ {0,3}(#{1,6})(?:[ \t]+(.*))?$')
    fence_re = re.compile(r'^ {0,3}(`{3,}|~{3,})')

    results: List[Tuple[int, str]] = []
    in_fence: bool = False
    fence_char: str = ''

    for line in markdown.splitlines():
        # Check for fence open/close
        fm = fence_re.match(line)
        if fm is not None:
            fence_marker = fm.group(1)
            if not in_fence:
                in_fence = True
                fence_char = fence_marker[0]
            elif fence_char == fence_marker[0]:
                in_fence = False
                fence_char = ''
            continue

        if in_fence:
            continue

        m = heading_re.match(line)
        if m is None:
            continue
        level = len(m.group(1))
        raw_title = m.group(2)
        if raw_title is None:
            title = ""
        else:
            title = raw_title.strip()
            # Drop optional closing run of '#' chars when preceded by space or is the whole title
            if title:
                stripped = re.sub(r'[ \t]+#+$', '', title)
                if stripped != title:
                    title = stripped.strip()
                if title and re.fullmatch(r'#+', title):
                    title = ""
        results.append((level, title))
    return results
"}}, "messages": []}
